bull_thesis:
The bull case is that Figma's shares were broken by plumbing rather than by business decay, and that the plumbing has a contractual end date four trading days away.

Start with the business, because the whole case rests on it being healthy. Revenue in the quarter ended 31 March 2026 was $333.4 million, up 46% from a year earlier -- and that growth rate went 38%, then 40%, then 46% across the last three reported quarters. It accelerated during exactly the months the market was pricing the company as roadkill. Net dollar retention, which measures how much existing customers spend now versus a year ago, reached 139%, the highest in more than two years. Management raised full-year 2026 guidance to $1.422-1.428 billion, about 35% growth, and lifted adjusted operating income guidance to $125-135 million. Free cash flow over the last four reported quarters totals about $237 million. Cash and short-term investments stood at $1.638 billion against $56.2 million of debt, so roughly $3.00 a share of net cash and no solvency question of any kind.

Now the plumbing. Figma came public on 31 July 2025 with a very small tradable float and an unusually elaborate lock-up -- the window during which insiders and pre-listing investors are barred from selling. The original 180-day lock-up ran out on 27 January 2026. A second agreement signed on 30 August 2025 covering about 54.1% of the Class A shares set up four further releases tied to earnings dates: about 38.9 million shares in November 2025, 44.4 million in February 2026, 61.1 million in May 2026, and the final and largest tranche of about 77.7 million shares at the open on the second trading day after the June-quarter report. The company confirmed on 15 July 2026 that it reports after the close on Wednesday 5 August 2026, which fixes that final release at Friday 7 August 2026.

The bull sequence is therefore simple and dated. Ten months of near-continuous, price-insensitive supply from venture funds distributing stock to their limited partners ends permanently on 7 August. What is left is a business growing in the high-30s with 139% retention, a $1.6 billion cash pile, an engaged activist (Findell Capital, whose June 2026 letter demands the product line be cut from eight offerings to four and carries a $40 target), and a share register finally free to be set by fundamental buyers rather than by mechanical sellers. The stock closed 31 July 2026 at $24.32, about 83% below its first-month peak of $142.92 and 26% below its $33 offering price, valuing the operating business at roughly 7.9 times this year's guided revenue. Sentiment does not need to improve for that to re-rate toward $29-30; the selling merely has to stop.

The conditions this case requires: the 5 August print must confirm the guided $348-350 million and roughly 40% growth; the 7 August release must be absorbed in days rather than months; and the market's fear that generative artificial intelligence makes design software unnecessary must stay a narrative rather than showing up in the retention numbers.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is that the event points the wrong way, the entry price has already moved against us, and the floor underneath the position is demonstrated rather than defined.

Direction first. A forced-seller trade pays when a known seller is exhausted and the price is then free to rise. What is contractually certain on 7 August 2026 is not exhaustion -- it is the arrival of permission to sell for about 77.7 million shares, roughly 15% of the ~528 million shares outstanding and a far larger share of what actually trades daily. These holders are pre-listing venture funds, which typically distribute stock in kind to their limited partners, who then liquidate on their own schedule with no reference to price. That is why each of the three earlier tranches produced weeks of drift rather than a single clean flush. Buying on 3 August is buying four days ahead of the largest wave of supply in the company's public life, not after it.

Price second, and this is decisive. The board file underwrites a $29.00 target, a $17.50 floor and a reward-to-risk multiple of 2.85. Those three numbers are only mutually consistent at a share price near $20.49 -- roughly where the stock sat when the file was struck. Since then it has rallied about 46% off its $16.60 record low to $24.32. Against the verified $16.60 low the same target now gives about 19% of upside versus about 32% of downside, a ratio of roughly 0.6 to 1 pointing the wrong way. The rally did not confirm the thesis; it consumed it.

Third, there is no real floor. This is not a signed merger, not a company trading below net cash, not a liquidation. Net cash of about $3.00 a share is 12% of the price and backstops nothing. The only thing under the stock is the $16.60 printed in early July 2026 and re-tested to form a double bottom -- a level the market recently paid, not a level anything prevents it going through. At $16.60 the operating business would be valued at about 5.0 times this year's guided revenue and 4.1 times the roughly $1.76 billion the street models for 2027, which is a perfectly reachable price if the terminal-value argument gains any further ground.

Fourth, the economics behind the growth are deteriorating. Reported gross margin has fallen from about 92% in late 2024 to 79.4% in the March 2026 quarter; some of that is post-listing stock compensation in cost of revenue, but part is the cost of serving artificial-intelligence features and does not reverse. Stock-based compensation was $169.0 million in that single quarter, about 51% of revenue; the activist's own full-year estimate is 27% of revenue against 8% at Adobe. The share count went from 474.8 million to 523.5 million in a year, about 10%. So the claim that the overhang clears for good on 7 August is wrong in a specific way: the contractual overhang clears, the structural issuance of roughly a tenth of the company a year does not.

Finally, the secular fear is live and the market acts on it without warning. Shares fell about 16.5% in the week to 24 July 2026 on generative-artificial-intelligence displacement worry with no company news at all, after a competing design tool launched in April 2026. The sell side has been walking its target down, from about $40 in March 2026 to roughly $30.40 in late July, on a book of four Buys, one Outperform and eight Holds. What confirms this case: any deceleration below the guided 40% on 5 August, retention slipping from 139%, or the 7 August tape showing heavy volume with the price giving back the July rally.

positioning_washout:
Forced selling is the entire thesis on this name, and for the first time it has a termination date rather than an open end. Understanding exactly who is selling is what separates the good version of this trade from the bad one.

The sellers are not disappointed fundamental holders and not a yield-focused base being forced out by a dividend cut. They are pre-listing venture funds and early employees. Venture funds rarely sell in the ordinary sense: they distribute shares in kind to their limited partners -- pension plans, endowments, funds of funds -- who then liquidate on their own timetable, often through a broker with instructions to complete rather than to achieve a price. That flow is genuinely price-insensitive, which is why it can push a stock far below any reasonable value and why it takes weeks to clear rather than days.

The sequence so far: the original 180-day lock-up expired 27 January 2026, freeing roughly two-thirds of the share count. On top of it, four staged tranches of the 54.1% extended block released about 38.9 million shares in November 2025, 44.4 million in February 2026 and 61.1 million in May 2026. Each was followed by drift. The stock made its record low of $16.60 in early July, about six weeks after the May tranche -- which is roughly how long that supply took to work through.

The employee side is a distinct and colder story. Staff watched roughly 80% of the paper value of their holdings evaporate between the August 2025 peak and the January 2026 unlock, when the stock was near $22.51. That cohort is not selling to take profits; it is selling to salvage. That behaviour is insensitive to the fundamental case and to good news.

What happens after 7 August is the honest open question. The optimistic reading is that the last identified seller is released, the register turns over to fundamental holders, and the drift ends. The realistic reading is that release is not exhaustion -- the shares merely become sellable, and the distribution-to-limited-partner chain then runs for weeks. The washout that would make this a buy is the tape from roughly 7 to 21 August: heavy volume, a decisive break of the $16.60-18.00 shelf, and then a failure to make a new low. That is a specific, observable event, and it has not happened.

# FIG (Figma, Inc.) -- Forensic dossier: a forced-seller special situation

Event-driven review, verified live on 3 August 2026. The question in front of this committee is not whether Figma is a good business. It is whether the gap between Friday's close of $24.32 and a plausible event-resolved value is wide enough, and whether the event that is supposed to close that gap is real, dated and pointed in the right direction.

The short answer, established below and then tested in every section: the event is real, it is contractually dated to Friday 7 August 2026, and it is the largest single release of stock in the company's short public life. But it is a supply event arriving into a price that has already risen about 46% off its record low in four weeks. The asymmetry the board file was underwriting has been spent by the rally, and the supply has not yet landed.

## 1. Narrative arc -- how the setup got here

Figma listed on the New York Stock Exchange on 31 July 2025 at $33 a share and traded to an intraday $142.92 in its first weeks. It closed Friday 31 July 2026 at $24.32. That divergence is the whole reason this name is in front of us, and it has two causes that must be kept separate because they call for opposite conclusions.

Each tranche is tied to an earnings announcement: about 38.9 million shares (17.5% of the block) after the third-quarter 2025 report, released November 2025; about 44.4 million (20%) after the full-year 2025 report, released February 2026; about 61.1 million (27.5%) after the first-quarter 2026 report, released May 2026; and about 77.7 million (35%) at the open on the second trading day after the second-quarter 2026 report, or 31 August 2026 if that comes first -- pending, and dated 7 August 2026.

Figma confirmed on 15 July 2026 that it will report the June quarter after the close on Wednesday 5 August 2026. Two trading days later is Friday 7 August 2026. That is the date. It is not an estimate, a guidance range or a management aspiration; it is a contractual trigger disclosed in a filed 8-K, and the only way it moves is if the earnings date moves, in which case the backstop of 31 August 2026 applies.

The second cause is a genuine argument about the future. Since roughly April 2026 the market has been pricing design software as a category that generative artificial intelligence may make cheap or unnecessary. A competitor's launch of a rival design tool in April 2026 is the specific event that crystallised that fear for this stock. The record low of $16.60 was printed in early July.

The rally back to $24.32 came from three things: a double bottom in the chart around $16.60-18.00, a reinstated Buy from Bank of America, and an activist campaign that put a $40 target on the tape. None of those is the lock-up.

The arc, stated plainly: a healthy business was repriced by a combination of mechanical supply and a legitimate secular fear, and it has already bounced hard into the last, largest tranche of that supply.

## 2. Is the catalyst real, dated and binding?

Yes on all three counts, with one important qualification.

Real and dated. The release is documented in the 8-K covering the 30 August 2025 extended lock-up agreement. The trigger is mechanical. The date, 7 August 2026, is four days from now.

Binding. The holders are released; nothing compels them to sell. That is the qualification, and it cuts in a specific direction that the bull case usually gets backwards. The event that is contractually certain is the arrival of permission to sell. What the thesis actually needs is the exhaustion of the sellers, and that is not contractual at all. It is an empirical question about how quickly roughly 77.7 million shares -- about 15% of the ~528 million shares outstanding, and a far larger fraction of the shares that actually trade -- are absorbed.

## 3. Sponsor and management credibility on hitting the date

There is no sponsor to handicap here, and that is a point in the setup's favour: no acquirer can walk, no regulator can issue a second request, no trial can miss its endpoint. The date arrives on its own.

Management credibility matters for the other event in the same week -- the 5 August earnings report -- and the record there is good but short. On the narrow question of whether they hit their own number on 5 August, the honest answer is that they probably will. Reliability: high, on a short record.

## 4. The verified downside floor -- what actually backstops the price

This is where the setup is weakest, and the committee should not be talked out of it.

The analyst target has been walking down, not up: the mean price target fell from about $40 in March 2026 to roughly $30.40 in late July, and the rating book is now four Buys, one Outperform and eight Holds. The sell side is not the source of the bounce.
